extracted.intended_audience: high-school / introductory creative-writing students (AP English learners) and beginning fiction writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating vivid, immersive settings in fiction by establishing time/place, cultural context, sensory detail, atmosphere, and spatial relationships so the setting shapes character and theme. Intended as an introductory how-to for students learning descriptive technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting (definition & layers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting refers to the time and place in which a story occurs. It has several layers, and the strongest settings address most or all of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that setting is more than backdrop: it's the foundation that shapes character behavior, choices, and reader feeling. Treat setting as the world the reader agrees to step into.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time period
rubrics_metrics.description: Time period — historical, contemporary, or futuristic. The era you choose influences everything: your characters' attitudes, values, speech patterns, and daily routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use period-specific details (technology, fashion, popular culture) to signal when the reader is without explicit announcement; choose cultural details that actually matter to your characters and story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic location
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic location — a specific country, region, city, or neighborhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounding the story in a recognizable (or carefully invented) place gives readers something to hold onto and orients them in space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical environment — landscapes, weather, architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These details orient the reader and reflect mood and theme (e.g., a desolate wasteland vs. a bustling metropolis). Use particulars rather than generic descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social norms and customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Social norms and customs shape how characters interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different eras or cultures have different behavioral rules; these should inform character choices and interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical events and political climate
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical events and political climate can drive your plot or pressure your characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relevant events (e.g., wars, social movements) to create built-in tension or moral stakes in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic conditions and class structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic conditions and class structures affect what your characters can and can't do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete constraints (e.g., Great Depression limiting opportunity, dystopian hierarchies) should inform plot options and character goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period-specific details
rubrics_metrics.description: Period-specific details like technology, fashion, and popular culture make a setting feel authentic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small touches (horse-drawn carriages, flapper dresses, disco music) signal time; but 'don't just sprinkle in historical facts for decoration' — choose details that matter to characters and story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Mood is the emotional tone your story evokes in the reader — suspense, romance, melancholy, unease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selection of sensory details and descriptive language to evoke a consistent emotional tone across scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Atmosphere is the overall feeling of a setting, built through your selection of sensory details and descriptive language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools include lighting/color, weather/natural phenomena, and selective detail. Be intentional and avoid overused tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighting and color
rubrics_metrics.description: Lighting and color choices suggest mood (e.g., warm golden hues for nostalgia, cool blue tones for distance or sadness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use color and light deliberately to support atmosphere; specific examples given (warm = comfort, cool = sadness, harsh fluorescent = clinical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather and natural phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Weather and natural phenomena amplify or soften emotion in a scene (e.g., thunderstorm during confrontation, snowfall during reunion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective but can become cliché if overused — deploy with intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective detail
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't need to describe everything; the details you choose to include tell the reader how to feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selective, distinctive details (an eerie fog vs. a firelit cabin) create contrasting atmospheres. Avoid catalog-like description; focus on what matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong settings appeal to more than sight. Engaging all five senses pulls readers deeper into the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sight is default but should be specific; include sound, smell, touch, and occasionally taste. 'Challenge yourself to include at least two non-visual senses in every major setting passage.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sight (sensory detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual description should be specific (e.g., 'a dilapidated Victorian mansion with peeling paint and overgrown ivy' rather than 'an old house').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete nouns and images to create a clear picture rather than vague adjectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound (sensory detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound adds realism and emotional texture (e.g., tolling church bells vs. lively marketplace chatter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sounds that reinforce mood or signal activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smell (sensory detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smell is uniquely powerful because it triggers memory and association (e.g., fresh bread vs. acrid polluted river).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scent to evoke emotion and memory connections in the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touch (sensory detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Touch makes a setting tangible (e.g., rough tree bark, cool marble surface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactile details ground the reader's body in the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste (sensory detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is used less often but can be striking (e.g., dust on the tongue during a drought, salt spray near the ocean).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ taste sparingly for high-impact moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid visual-only description
rubrics_metrics.description: A common beginner mistake is relying almost entirely on visual description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include at least two non-visual senses in every major setting passage to avoid flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose strong verbs and nouns before modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Vivid settings come from precise, specific word choices — not from piling on adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer strong verbs/nouns ('the door groaned open') over adjective-heavy phrasing ('the old door slowly opened').

rubrics_metrics.name: Figurative language
rubrics_metrics.description: Similes, metaphors, and personification give readers a fresh way to see something (e.g., 'the moon hung like a silver medallion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figurative language to make settings memorable and to link sensory experience to theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory language (as technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensory language keeps the reader grounded in experience rather than abstraction (e.g., 'pungent aroma of spices' or 'velvety softness of rose petals').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concrete sensory phrasing over abstract descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism in setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolism connects setting to theme (e.g., barren landscape mirroring emotional emptiness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make setting part of story's meaning, not just its container; use symbolic elements deliberately to reinforce theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: How you arrange and frame elements of a setting creates a sense of real, three-dimensional space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relationships between objects and locations to add depth (e.g., skyscrapers looming over winding streets gives scale and enclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective and point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspective and point of view shape what the reader notices (a child's eye-level vs. adult's; bird's-eye view creates distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe spaces through the vantage point of the POV character to reveal different details and emotional orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale and proportion emphasize what matters (e.g., a tiny hut dwarfed by ancient forest suggests vulnerability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulate relative sizes to convey theme or character status quickly and visually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movement through space
rubrics_metrics.description: Movement through space makes settings dynamic rather than static.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show characters moving (climbing a steep path, weaving through a train station) to keep description active and avoid catalog-style listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immersion as the goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the reader forget they're reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A setting that feels real gives characters a world worth inhabiting and readers a world worth visiting; integrate setting with character, action, and theme to achieve immersion.
